variants.title: Run the measurement pipeline
variants.context: A benchmark result is the end of a four-stage pipeline: freeze the task manifest, generate under one contract, extract and verify the final answer, then aggregate with slices. Each stage can change the score, so each belongs in the run manifest.
variants.prompt: A team wants a reproducible GSM8K number for a new model build. Put the pipeline stages in order.

items.text: Generate every response under one pinned prompt, model revision, decoding setting, candidate count, and token budget.
Freeze the task manifest: dataset revision, split, task IDs, exclusions, and contamination policy.
Extract the declared final-answer field, normalize only allowed forms, and compare under explicit assumptions.
Aggregate accuracy with denominators, uncertainty, slices, cost, exclusions, and verifier failures together.

variants.hint: The manifest exists before the first response is generated.
variants.explanation: Dataset, inference, scoring, claim: the order guarantees that the reported number can be traced back to a frozen experiment.

variants.title: Run the measurement pipeline
variants.context: A benchmark result is the end of a four-stage pipeline: freeze the task manifest, generate under one contract, extract and verify the final answer, then aggregate with slices. Each stage can change the score, so each belongs in the run manifest.
variants.prompt: The team changes the prompt demonstrations for MATH. Put the steps in order so the new result is a new versioned experiment rather than an edit to the old one.

items.text: Extract and verify with the same versioned parser so the scorer is not a second change.
Aggregate by subject and difficulty and compare against the old run only with both manifests beside each other.
Regenerate all responses under the new prompt with the same model, decoding, and token budget as before.
Record the new demonstrations in a new frozen manifest instead of editing the old run's record.

variants.hint: A prompt change is a new manifest, and only one thing should change at a time.
variants.explanation: Prompt demonstrations move the score without any model change, so the run gets its own manifest and the comparison keeps both manifests visible.

variants.title: Run the measurement pipeline
variants.context: A benchmark result is the end of a four-stage pipeline: freeze the task manifest, generate under one contract, extract and verify the final answer, then aggregate with slices. Each stage can change the score, so each belongs in the run manifest.
variants.prompt: After a model change, the team must not only report accuracy but also watch for scorer problems. Put the full operational sequence in order.

items.text: Extract the final field and record parse_failure for every response without one.
Aggregate accuracy with slices and the parse-failure rate in the same report.
Generate under the pinned prompt, decoding settings, and candidate count.
Freeze the task manifest with the dataset revision, split, and contamination policy.
Alert on score changes together with parse-failure rate, slice regressions, and verifier timeouts.
Manually audit a bounded sample of passes and failures after the change.

variants.hint: The audit comes after the numbers exist, and the alert compares numbers to prior runs.
variants.explanation: Parse failures are retained during extraction, reported alongside accuracy, alerted on, and then checked by a bounded manual audit.

variants.title: Score one response fail-closed
variants.context: Fail-closed scoring extracts a declared final field first, records parse_failure when it is missing, normalizes only declared syntax, parses into an exact value, and compares under explicit assumptions. Sets, intervals, and units stay semantically distinct from a single scalar.
variants.prompt: A response ends with the declared final field holding a boxed value written as 1,000, and the gold answer is 1000. Put the scoring steps in order.

items.text: Normalize the comma and surrounding whitespace, which are explicitly allowed.
Locate the declared final field at the end of the response.
Parse the string into an exact numeric value.
Remove the documented boxed wrapper, which is presentation only.
Compare the parsed value with the gold value and record the verdict with the parser version.

variants.hint: Wrappers come off before syntax is normalized, and normalization happens before parsing.
variants.explanation: Extraction, wrapper removal, declared normalization, exact parsing, then comparison: each step only touches what the contract allows.

variants.title: Score one response fail-closed
variants.context: Fail-closed scoring extracts a declared final field first, records parse_failure when it is missing, normalizes only declared syntax, parses into an exact value, and compares under explicit assumptions. Sets, intervals, and units stay semantically distinct from a single scalar.
variants.prompt: A response explains the solution, mentions 42 twice, corrects itself to 40, but never writes the required final field. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Do not scan the explanation for a convenient number.
Search for the declared final-answer delimiter.
Keep the task in the denominator and count it in the parse-failure rate.
Retain the raw output so the failure can be audited later.
Record parse_failure because the field is absent.

variants.hint: The explanation contains candidate numbers, and the contract says what to do with them.
variants.explanation: Missing final fields are recorded as parse_failure and kept in the denominator; searching the prose would reward whichever number the scorer happened to find.

variants.title: Score one response fail-closed
variants.context: Fail-closed scoring extracts a declared final field first, records parse_failure when it is missing, normalizes only declared syntax, parses into an exact value, and compares under explicit assumptions. Sets, intervals, and units stay semantically distinct from a single scalar.
variants.prompt: The task asks for all real solutions of x squared equals 4, and the response's final field is the set {-2, 2}. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Compare for completeness against the gold set under the stated real-number assumption.
Parse each element into an exact numeric value.
Extract the final field as written.
Recognize the value as a set of two roots, not a single scalar.
Record the verdict and keep the set semantics in the retained record.

variants.hint: A scalar parser would accept an incomplete answer; the type of the answer is decided before parsing.
variants.explanation: Set-valued answers are kept semantically distinct from scalars, so completeness is part of the comparison rather than collapsed into one number.

variants.title: Do the item math
variants.context: The lesson reads two items as structured tasks. In an angle-bisector problem the bisector from A splits BC so that BD / DC = AB / AC. In a GSM8K item the words translate into one executable relation, such as (16 - 3 - 4) x 2 = 18.
variants.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = 10, AC = 15, and BC = 20. The bisector from A meets BC at D. What is BD?
variants.hint: Split BC in the ratio AB to AC.
variants.explanation: BD / DC = 10 / 15 = 2 / 3, and BD + DC = 20, so BD = 8 and DC = 12.

mistakes.feedback: That is DC; BD is the part next to B, the shorter part because AB is shorter than AC.
That copies AB; BD is a segment of BC, found from the ratio.

variants.title: Do the item math
variants.context: The lesson reads two items as structured tasks. In an angle-bisector problem the bisector from A splits BC so that BD / DC = AB / AC. In a GSM8K item the words translate into one executable relation, such as (16 - 3 - 4) x 2 = 18.
variants.prompt: A farm produces 24 eggs. 5 are eaten, 7 are used for baking, and each remaining egg sells for 3 dollars. How many dollars does the farm earn?
variants.hint: Find the remaining inventory before you multiply.

mistakes.feedback: Interpretation error: the consumed eggs were added instead of subtracted.
Planning error: the response multiplied before subtracting the consumed eggs.

variants.context: The lesson reads two items as structured tasks. In an angle-bisector problem the bisector from A splits BC so that BD / DC = AB / AC. In a GSM8K item the words translate into one executable relation, such as (16 - 3 - 4) x 2 = 18.
variants.prompt: The MATH manifest lists 12,500 problems, of which 7,500 are training problems. What percent of the release is the test split?
variants.hint: Test problems divided by all problems.

mistakes.feedback: That divides test by train instead of by the whole release.

variants.title: Classify the GSM8K failure
variants.context: A GSM8K error taxonomy separates four causes: interpretation errors choose the wrong relation, planning errors order the operations wrongly, execution errors get an intermediate arithmetic step wrong, and answer-contract errors get the mathematics right but fail extraction or formatting.
variants.prompt: For the eggs item, a response computes (16 + 3 + 4) x 2 = 46. Which failure class is it?
options: Interpretation error: consumed eggs were added instead of subtracted.
Execution error: the operations were right but the arithmetic slipped.
Answer-contract error: the final field was formatted incorrectly.
optionFeedback: The relation itself is wrong; the response misread what happens to eaten and baked eggs.
The arithmetic is correct for the relation chosen; the relation is the problem.
Nothing about formatting failed; the mathematics was set up wrongly.
variants.hint: Was the wrong operation chosen, or was a right operation computed wrongly?
variants.explanation: Adding consumed eggs is an interpretation error, because the response translated the words into the wrong relation.

variants.title: Classify the GSM8K failure
variants.context: A GSM8K error taxonomy separates four causes: interpretation errors choose the wrong relation, planning errors order the operations wrongly, execution errors get an intermediate arithmetic step wrong, and answer-contract errors get the mathematics right but fail extraction or formatting.
variants.prompt: A response sets up 16 - 3 - 4 = 9 and then 9 x 2 = 16, and reports 16. Which failure class is it?
options: Execution error: the plan was right but an arithmetic step was wrong.
Interpretation error: the response misread the problem.
Planning error: the operations were applied in the wrong order.
optionFeedback: The selected operations are right; 9 x 2 is simply miscomputed.
The relation matches the problem; only the arithmetic failed.
The order is correct: subtract, then multiply.
variants.hint: Check the plan first, then check each computed step.
variants.explanation: When the relation and order are right but an intermediate arithmetic step is wrong, the class is execution error.

variants.title: Classify the GSM8K failure
variants.context: A GSM8K error taxonomy separates four causes: interpretation errors choose the wrong relation, planning errors order the operations wrongly, execution errors get an intermediate arithmetic step wrong, and answer-contract errors get the mathematics right but fail extraction or formatting.
variants.prompt: A response derives 18 correctly with a valid explanation but writes the answer as 'eighteen eggs' without the required final field. The scorer records parse_failure. Which failure class is it?
options: Execution error: the response computed something wrong.
Interpretation error: the response answered the wrong question.
Answer-contract error: the mathematics is right but extraction failed.
optionFeedback: The computation was correct; the failure came after the mathematics.
The response answered the right question correctly.
The parser could not extract the declared field, which is exactly the answer-contract class.
variants.hint: Where in the pipeline did the correct answer get lost?
variants.explanation: A correct derivation that fails extraction or formatting is an answer-contract error, and it should be reported as a parse failure rather than a reasoning failure.

variants.title: Keep the headline reproducible
variants.context: The original benchmark accuracy stays reproducible under its declared scorer. Stricter symbolic, trace, robustness, or product diagnostics are added as separate metrics, parser changes are versioned and audited, and dropped tasks never leave the denominator silently.
variants.prompt: A team wants the MATH headline score to accept a broader set of symbolically equivalent expressions than the declared scorer does. Where does the broader check belong?
options: In the headline score, since equivalence is mathematically correct.
As a separate named metric beside the reproducible headline.
Nowhere; only the original scorer is ever allowed.
optionFeedback: Broad simplification can introduce false positives and silently changes what the headline means.
Additional checks are reported separately so the original number stays comparable.
Extra diagnostics are encouraged; they simply must not replace the declared scorer.
variants.hint: What happens to comparability if the headline scorer changes?
variants.explanation: Add stricter or broader diagnostics as separate metrics instead of silently changing the headline score.

variants.title: Keep the headline reproducible
variants.context: The original benchmark accuracy stays reproducible under its declared scorer. Stricter symbolic, trace, robustness, or product diagnostics are added as separate metrics, parser changes are versioned and audited, and dropped tasks never leave the denominator silently.
variants.prompt: The parser is upgraded to handle fractions. The model has not changed. What must happen before the new score is compared with last week's?
options: Nothing; the model is the same so the scores are comparable.
Drop every task the old parser failed on so both runs share a denominator.
Version the parser, run it on the fixture set, and manually audit a bounded sample of passes and failures.
optionFeedback: A parser change can move the score without any model change.
Excluding tasks silently changes the denominator; failures belong in the report.
Parser changes are treated like model changes: versioned, tested on fixtures, and audited.
variants.hint: Which pipeline stage changed, and does the lesson treat that as a real change?
variants.explanation: Any prompt, parser, model, or dataset change triggers a versioned run, fixture tests, and a bounded manual audit before comparison.

variants.title: Keep the headline reproducible
variants.context: The original benchmark accuracy stays reproducible under its declared scorer. Stricter symbolic, trace, robustness, or product diagnostics are added as separate metrics, parser changes are versioned and audited, and dropped tasks never leave the denominator silently.
variants.prompt: A report shows 91 percent MATH accuracy but excludes 8 percent of tasks that produced symbolic-checker timeouts. How should the number be presented?
options: As 91 percent, since timeouts are evaluator problems, not model problems.
With the exact denominator, the timeout count, and the timeout rate reported beside the accuracy.
As 83 percent, by counting every timeout as a wrong answer with no further note.
optionFeedback: Hidden exclusions make the score irreproducible and inflate it.
The score vector includes parse failures, timeouts, invalid outputs, and dropped tasks with the denominator.
Timeouts need their own count; folding them into wrong answers hides a verifier failure.
variants.hint: The lesson publishes the score as a vector, not a single number.
variants.explanation: Report denominators, timeouts, parse failures, and exclusions together so the reader can see what the accuracy covers.
